svg.data-vd-play-label: Play: the journey of a meal through the gut
svg.data-vd-steps: [[0, "Ingestion. Teeth cut and grind the food (mechanical digestion) and the tongue shapes it into a bolus. Saliva moistens it, and salivary amylase starts to digest starch into maltose."], [3, "Swallowing. The bolus passes through the pharynx into the oesophagus. Peristalsis, waves of muscle contraction behind the bolus, pushes it down to the stomach."], [6.5, "Stomach. The muscular wall churns the food with gastric juice: hydrochloric acid kills microorganisms and gives the low pH at which the protease pepsin starts digesting proteins. The food becomes liquid chyme."], [10, "Duodenum. The pyloric sphincter releases chyme a little at a time. Bile from the gall bladder neutralises the acid and emulsifies fats; pancreatic juice adds amylase, protease and lipase."], [13.5, "Small intestine. Digestion is completed, and the small, soluble products (glucose, amino acids, fatty acids and glycerol) are absorbed through the villi into the blood and lymph."], [16.5, "Large intestine. Most of the remaining water is absorbed. Undigested material (mainly fibre) forms faeces, stored in the rectum and egested through the anus."]]
svg.title: The human digestive system
svg.desc: Front view of the human digestive system: mouth, salivary glands, pharynx, oesophagus, stomach, liver, gall bladder, bile duct, pancreas, duodenum, small intestine, caecum, appendix, colon, rectum and anus, with the diaphragm for position.
svg.text: Front view: the body’s right side is on the left of the diagram. Organs simplified; not to scale.

g.data-info: Sheet of muscle separating the thorax from the abdomen; the oesophagus passes through it. Not part of the digestive system: shown for position.
Three pairs of glands (parotid, submandibular, sublingual) whose ducts release saliva into the mouth: water, mucus and salivary amylase.
Ingestion. Teeth cut and grind food (mechanical digestion), increasing its surface area; the tongue rolls it into a bolus; saliva moistens it and its amylase starts digesting starch.
The throat: shared by food and air. When you swallow, the epiglottis covers the trachea so the bolus goes into the oesophagus.
A muscular tube (about 25 cm) from the pharynx to the stomach. Waves of contraction of its circular and longitudinal muscle (peristalsis) push the bolus down. No digestion happens here.
Gland behind the stomach. Its pancreatic juice (amylase, protease, lipase and hydrogencarbonate) flows into the duodenum. It also makes the hormones insulin and glucagon.

Muscular bag on the left of the abdomen. Its wall churns food; gastric juice adds hydrochloric acid (pH about 2, kills microorganisms) and protease (pepsin), which begins protein digestion. Food leaves as chyme.
Ring of muscle at the exit of the stomach that lets small amounts of chyme into the duodenum at a time.

About 6 m long and coiled. Digestion is completed by enzymes on the epithelium; villi and microvilli give a huge surface for absorbing glucose, amino acids, fatty acids, glycerol, vitamins and minerals into blood and lymph.
First part of the small intestine, a C-shaped loop. Receives chyme from the stomach, bile and pancreatic juice; digestion of starch, proteins and fats continues here.
The largest gland, under the diaphragm on the right. Makes bile; also stores glycogen, breaks down excess amino acids (deamination, making urea) and removes toxins.
Stores bile made by the liver and releases it into the duodenum through the bile duct after a meal.
Carries bile to the duodenum. Bile is alkaline (neutralises stomach acid) and emulsifies fats into small droplets, increasing the surface area for lipase.
Ascending, transverse, descending and sigmoid colon. Absorbs most of the remaining water and some mineral ions, forming faeces; bacteria here make some vitamins (e.g. vitamin K).
Pouch at the start of the large intestine, where the ileum joins it (lower right of the body).
Narrow, closed-ended tube attached to the caecum. No digestive role in humans; contains lymphoid tissue.
Stores faeces until they are egested.
Opening controlled by sphincter muscles through which faeces leave the body (egestion).
